flatness-threshold-critical.title: The Flatness Threshold and Critical Density
flatness-threshold-critical.content:
Cosmological mass-energy density required to establish a flat spatial geometry under General Relativistic Friedmann dynamics is defined by the critical threshold. In active cosmological models, this density is compared to the actual density of the universe through the total density parameter \( \Omega \), which is parameterized by Expansion Parameters (\(q\) and \(w\)) that govern the deceleration and pressure of the cosmic fluid. If the actual density exceeds this threshold, the spatial coordinates curve positively to form a closed universe, whereas a deficit results in an open, negatively curved geometry. In early cosmic epochs, the total mass-energy was dominated by baryons and dark matter, including relativistic components like neutrino species that constitute Hot Dark Matter (HDM). Under these expanding conditions, the cosmic density is written as the critical value

\[ ho_c = rac{3 H(t)^2}{8\pi G} \]

where \( ho_c \) represents the critical density, \( H(t) \) is the time-dependent expansion rate, and \( G \) is the gravitational constant. This mathematical boundary separates the different geometric fates of the spatial grid, showing that flatness is a highly unstable equilibrium under standard gravity.

To construct a formal variational foundation for this critical density, the transport of the cosmic fluid is modeled using the covariant stress-energy tensor. In relativistic kinematics, the energy and momentum of all physical particles must satisfy Energy-Momentum Relation \( p^\mu p_\mu = -m^2 c^2 \), which limits the local propagation of mass-energy to the light cone. Within the curved FLRW spacetime, the stress-energy tensor \( T^{\mu u} = ( ho + P/c^2) U^\mu U^ u + P g_{\mu u} \) couples the pressure \( P \) and density \( ho \) directly to the metric tensor \( g_{\mu u} \), forcing the expansion rate to adapt to the total density. By enforcing the covariant conservation law \( abla_\mu T^{\mu u} = 0 \), the theory guarantees that the local mass-energy remains conserved, proving that the flatness threshold is a direct consequence of general relativistic energy conservation.

The physical constituents of this mass-energy density consist primarily of non-baryonic dark matter, whose properties are modeled as cold, collisionless particles such as WIMPs (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles). Unlike the dense baryonic matter that forms the neutron stars involved in GW170817: The Multi-Messenger Landmark, dark matter particles do not interact electromagnetically, meaning they only couple to the spatial geometry via their gravitational field, providing the primary invisible scaffold that governs the formation of cosmic structures. This non-baryonic matter provides the additional density \( ho_x \) required to bring the total density parameter closer to the flatness threshold, explaining why galaxy clusters and large-scale structures remain gravitationally bound despite the massive expansion of the background spatial grid, where their mass \( M \) and interaction cross section \( \sigma \) are constrained by laboratory searches, and their density \( ho_x \) provides the necessary gravitational potential.

The observational determination of this spatial curvature relies on measuring the expansion rate of the universe, which is parameterized by The Hubble Parameter (\(H\)). By measuring the angular diameter distance to the cosmic microwave background, cosmologists determined that the spatial curvature density parameter \( \Omega_k \equiv -k c^2 / a(t)^2 H(t)^2 \) is extremely close to zero, corresponding to a flat spatial geometry. This high-precision measurement requires that the expansion rate and total density satisfy the critical density relation at all epochs, proving that the flatness threshold is a robust, physically consistent, and coordinate-invariant representation of global cosmology, where the spatial curvature parameter \( k \), the speed of light \( c \), and the scale factor \( a(t) \) govern the curvature density parameter \( \Omega_k \) at any cosmic epoch.

The physical behavior of this density relation undergoes a continuous mathematical reduction in the late-time limiting case where the scale factor is formally taken to be infinitely large under accelerated expansion, corresponding to the limit \( a(t) o \infty \). In this dark-energy-dominated limit, the density of matter and radiation vanishes completely, and the total density parameter approaches unity as spatial curvature is smoothed out. Substituting the limit \( a(t) o \infty \) into these dynamic equations collapses the spatial curvature parameter directly to zero, \( \Omega_k o 0 \), where the universe becomes perfectly flat and expands exponentially at a constant rate \( H(t) o H_\infty \). The complex curved relation collapses smoothly to this flat de Sitter limit, demonstrating that spatial curvature cosmology reduces smoothly to a flat spatial geometry in the late-time limit, proving that the critical density is a robust, physically consistent, and coordinate-invariant representation of the universe across all stages of cosmic evolution.

identities.title: The Critical Density of the Universe
identities.description: Formulates the critical mass-energy density parameter that establishes the threshold between a closed, open, and flat spatial geometry.

equality-epoch.title: The Radiation-Matter Equality Epoch
equality-epoch.content:
Transition of the cosmic expansion from a radiation-dominated phase to a matter-dominated phase occurred when the energy density of relativistic species fell below that of non-relativistic matter. On stellar scales, this large-scale transition has no influence on local astrophysical structures, which are instead governed by hydrostatic equations or the degenerate dynamics that trigger Pulsar Glitches: Probing the Interior in neutron stars. On cosmological scales, however, this transition represents a fundamental shift in the behavior of Cosmic Gravity and the Scale Factor, as the expanding universe transitions from a decelerating radiation scaling to a slower matter-dominated deceleration. By requiring that the mass density of relativistic radiation and non-relativistic matter scale differently with the scale factor, the theory guarantees that the transition occurs at a unique value

\[ a_{ ext{eq}} = rac{\Omega_{r,0}}{\Omega_{m,0}} \]

where \( a_{ ext{eq}} \) represents the scale factor of radiation-matter equality, \( \Omega_{r,0} \) is the radiation density parameter at the present epoch, and \( \Omega_{m,0} \) is the matter density parameter, corresponding to a redshift of approximately \( z_{ ext{eq}} \approx 3400 \).

To construct a formal variational foundation for this equality epoch, the transport of the cosmic fluid is modeled using a multi-component stress-energy tensor that satisfies the Einstein equations. In relativistic mechanics, the energy and momentum of all physical components must obey Energy-Momentum Relation \( p^\mu p_\mu = -m^2 c^2 \), which limits the local propagation of relativistic radiation and non-relativistic matter. Within the curved spatial geometry, the total stress-energy tensor \( T^{\mu u} = T^{\mu u}_{ ext{radiation}} + T^{\mu u}_{ ext{matter}} \) couples the pressures and energy densities directly to the metric tensor \( g_{\mu u} \), forcing the global expansion rate to adapt to the dominant component. By enforcing the covariant conservation law \( abla_\mu T^{\mu u} = 0 \), the theory guarantees that the individual energy-momentum distributions remain conserved, proving that the equality epoch is a direct geometric consequence of general relativity.

The dominant component of this matter density consists primarily of non-baryonic Cold Dark Matter (CDM), whose gravitational collapse drives the hierarchical growth of all cosmic structures. The spatial distribution of this dark matter is observed across deep space using advanced observatories like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which maps the distribution of weak lensing and galaxy clusters to high redshifts \( z \). Before the equality epoch, the growth of these dark matter perturbations was heavily suppressed by the radiation pressure, whereas after equality, the perturbations began to grow gravitationally to form the cosmic web. This structural transition ensures that the observed galactic distribution remains entirely consistent with the cosmological parameters of the Lambda-CDM model, contributing to the total mass density \( ho_c \) and the matter parameter \( \Omega_m \), which maps the distribution of weak lensing.

The thermodynamic cooling of these relativistic and non-relativistic components as the universe expands is governed by the laws of Adiabatic Processes, which describe the scaling of temperature and entropy. Within this expanding background, the total entropy \( S \) of the cosmic fluid remains constant, forcing the radiation temperature to scale as \( T \propto a^{-1} \) and the radiation energy density to scale as \( ho_r \propto a^{-4} \). In contrast, the non-relativistic matter energy density scales as \( ho_m \propto a^{-3} \) due to volume expansion alone, without any redshift energy loss. This differential scaling is the fundamental physical driver of the equality epoch, ensuring that the radiation energy density must eventually fall below the matter density as the scale factor increases.

The physical behavior of this multi-component expansion relation undergoes a continuous mathematical reduction in the early-time limiting case where the scale factor is formally taken to be zero, corresponding to the limit \( a(t) o 0 \). In this early limit, the density of non-relativistic matter becomes completely negligible compared to the radiation density, and the universe enters the pure radiation-dominated era. Substituting the limit \( a(t) o 0 \) into these dynamic equations collapses the matter terms directly to the radiation-dominated limit, where the scale factor scales as \( a(t) \propto t^{1/2} \) and the expansion rate is governed by the Hubble parameter \( H(t) = rac{1}{2t} \). The complex multi-component relation collapses smoothly to this radiation limit, demonstrating that spatial cosmology reduces smoothly to a pure radiation fluid in the early-time limit, proving that the scale factor relation is a robust, physically consistent, and coordinate-invariant representation of cosmic evolution.

identities.title: The Scale Factor of Radiation-Matter Equality
identities.description: Formulates the cosmic scale factor at the epoch where the energy density of relativistic radiation falls exactly equal to that of non-relativistic matter.

radiation-domination.title: The Radiation-Dominated Era
radiation-domination.content:
Thermal history of the early universe during the first few hundred thousand years was dominated by highly relativistic particles whose energy density scaled inversely with the fourth power of the scale factor. On local stellar scales, the high-energy hydrodynamics of this hot plasma are modeled using the equations of Shock Waves that describe stellar explosions, which are fundamentally distinct from the smooth cosmological expansion. In the interior of compact remnants, the degenerate state is governed by the onset of Neutron Superfluidity, which provides frictionless flow uninfluenced by the hot radiation bath of the background. On global scales, however, this radiation-dominated expansion is characterized by the scaling laws \( a(t) \propto t^{1/2} \) and \( H(t) = rac{1}{2t} \), where the expansion rate depends on the effective relativistic degrees of freedom \( g_* \). Under these early conditions when the temperature \( T \sim 10^{10} ext{ K} \), the plasma was perfectly ionized, and the expansion was governed entirely by the energy density of photons and neutrinos.

To construct a formal variational foundation for this radiation era, the transport of the relativistic plasma is modeled using the stress-energy tensor of a perfect radiation fluid. In special relativity, the four-momentum of the relativistic photons and leptons must obey Energy-Momentum Relation \( p^\mu p_\mu = -m^2 c^2 \), which limits the local propagation of all physical information to the speed of light. Within the curved spatial geometry, the stress-energy tensor \( T^{\mu u} = ext{diag}(- ho, P, P, P) \) satisfies the radiation equation of state \( P = rac{1}{3} ho c^2 \), which couples the pressure directly to the energy density. By coupling this stress-energy tensor to the metric tensor \( g_{\mu u} \) through the Einstein equations, the theory guarantees that the local conservation of energy-momentum \( abla_\mu T^{\mu u} = 0 \) is satisfied throughout the pseudo-Riemannian manifold, providing a self-consistent representation of the expansion.

The thermodynamic behavior of this radiation era completely dominates over the dark energy term, which is modeled as a cosmological constant or a dynamic scalar field like Quintessence and Dynamical Dark Energy. Although dark energy dominates the energy budget in the modern epoch through the parameter \( \Omega_\Lambda \) or the constant \( \Lambda \), its physical influence was completely negligible during the early hot universe, where radiation density was trillions of times larger. Similarly, the cosmic magnetic fields present during this era were highly disordered and did not form the coherent magnetic structures governed by The Solar Dynamo that generate stellar fields \( B \). This radiation-dominated background provided a highly symmetric, homogeneous environment that allowed the synthesis of light elements to proceed uniformly across the observable universe.

The microscopic physical state of the leptons in this hot plasma is fundamentally different from the cold degenerate states found in compact stellar cores. Unlike white dwarf cores where the electrons are highly degenerate and their degeneracy pressure is modeled by Electron Degeneracy Pressure, the electrons and positrons in the early universe formed a hot, non-degenerate thermal gas. Under these relativistic conditions, the electron number density \( n_e \) and mass \( m_e \) were thermally balanced with the photons, and the Fermi energy played no role in the pressure equations. This thermal equilibrium ensured that the pressure was determined solely by the radiation equation of state, where the Planck constant \( \hbar \) and speed of light govern the thermal photon distribution.

The physical behavior of this radiation-dominated relation undergoes a continuous mathematical reduction in the late-time limiting case where the scale factor is formally taken to be infinitely large compared to its value at the present epoch, corresponding to the limit \( a(t) o \infty \). In this late-time limit, the radiation energy density vanishes completely, and the expansion of the universe transitions smoothly to the matter-dominated and eventually dark-energy-dominated eras. The Radiation Energy Density Scaling Law is formulated as the equation

\[ ho_r(a) = ho_{r,0} a^{-4} \]

where \( ho_r(a) \) represents the radiation energy density at any scale factor \( a(t) \), and \( ho_{r,0} \) is the radiation density parameter at the present epoch \( a_0 \). Substituting the late-time limit \( a(t) o \infty \) into this scaling relation collapses the radiation density directly to zero, \( ho_r o 0 \), where the cosmological dynamics are governed solely by matter and dark energy. The complex relativistic scaling relation collapses smoothly to this late-time limit, demonstrating that spatial cosmology reduces smoothly to a matter-dominated geometry as expansion proceeds, proving that the scaling law is a robust, physically consistent, and coordinate-invariant representation of the early universe.

identities.title: The Radiation Energy Density Scaling Law
identities.description: Formulates the scaling law for relativistic radiation energy density, showing that it decreases as the fourth power of the cosmic scale factor due to both volume expansion and wavelength stretching.
